title: Not seen by marks (section 5)
hook: can the Tathagata be known by bodily marks? no; where there are marks there is illusion

segments.voice: Yesterday, giving without resting on anything: give, and don't keep dwelling on the gift. Your line: boundless as space. What did you give and then leave alone? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-two.

A bronze Buddha sits behind museum glass. A rounded swell on the crown of the head. Long earlobes. Hair in small tight curls. A calm face, eyes half closed. Some of those features echo a list Buddhist tradition keeps: the marks of a great being, signs said to appear on the body of a Buddha. So here's a fair question, the kind a careful student might ask. If a Buddha has marks, is that how you recognize one? Section five of the Diamond Sutra asks exactly that, and the Buddha is the one asking. Today: not seen by marks.
screen: `A BRONZE BUDDHA BEHIND GLASS.` → `THE MARKS OF A GREAT BEING.` → `IS THAT HOW YOU KNOW ONE?`

segments.voice: First, the question. The Buddha turns to Subhuti and asks him: can the Tathagata be seen by means of his bodily marks? Tathagata is the name the Buddha uses for himself in the sutras. It's a test, and Subhuti doesn't take the easy answer. Second, the answer. No, Subhuti says. The Tathagata can't be seen by bodily marks, because the marks the Tathagata spoke of are no marks. Notice the shape of that sentence. The marks are named, and in the same breath they're said not to be what they seem. This sutra will do that again and again. Third, the line the whole section turns on. The Buddha agrees, and goes further. Wherever there are marks, he says, there is illusion. When you see that marks are no marks, you see the Tathagata. That's a paraphrase; the sutra's own words are short and strange, and translators put them differently. The point isn't that the statue is a lie, or that the body didn't matter. The sutra doesn't ask anyone to throw the statue out. It asks what you think you're seeing when you look at it. Fourth, the marks of a day. Much of a day runs on marks. A uniform tells you who to ask. An accent, a car, a job title, a wheelchair, a tattoo: each one gets sorted in half a second. The sorting is useful. It's also, this sutra says, where the illusion starts, because the person never fits inside the mark. The Diamond Sutra keeps cutting through that half second, and the first thing it cuts is the picture of the Buddha himself.
screen: `CAN HE BE SEEN BY HIS MARKS?` · `NO: THE MARKS ARE NO MARKS.` · `WHERE THERE ARE MARKS, ILLUSION.` · `THE HALF-SECOND SORT.` · then, large: `SEE NO-MARKS, SEE THE TATHAGATA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: see someone beyond appearance. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you know mostly by a mark: the neighbor with the loud truck, the coworker with the sharp voice, the cashier in the green vest. Name the marks you know them by, one on each out-breath, and set each one down. Then stay with what's left: someone who wakes up, gets tired, has a mother or had one, hopes the day goes well. You don't need to decide anything about them. Just look a little longer than half a second. When the marks come back, let them, and look past them again. The bell holds the time.
Not seen by marks. The Buddha isn't known by the body's signs; where there are marks, the sutra says, there is illusion. Today's word.
Your line: beyond the marks. Today, when you meet someone, notice the first mark you sort them by, a jacket, a voice, a job, and look one step past it. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: In Mahayana communities the Diamond Sutra is chanted, copied and studied, and a short passage like this one is often read slowly and talked over with a teacher.

fork.setup: you're Subhuti. the Buddha asks whether the Tathagata can be seen by his bodily marks. what do you answer?
options: yes: the marks are how a Buddha is known.
no: the marks he spoke of are no marks.
it depends on how good the statue is.
fork.reveal: Subhuti says no, and the Buddha goes further: wherever there are marks, there is illusion; see marks as no marks, and you see the Tathagata.

original.note: Sanskrit: a mark or sign; the word for the body's marks of a great being.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha had an ordinary body, nothing special to see.
what it means: the marks are there, but the Tathagata isn't known by them; where there are marks, there is illusion.
what a scholar hears: a thing named, then said to be no-thing: a pattern this sutra returns to in later sections.
recall: a factor that colors the knowing
